verdict: ENRICH concepts/data-rents.md (primary), research/tech-rent-dissolution-vs-capture.md, concepts/technofeudalism.md and concepts/rentier.md with 3-5 attributed sentences; do NOT create a book page now; do NOT create people/tim-wu.md. Reasons: (1) the book's contribution to the wiki is narrow and specific: a recognised antitrust scholar states on the record that his 'extraction' is the microeconomic monopoly rent (Lawfare transcript), which gives the wiki a Tier 1 named proponent of the rent reading of platform fees, with the trade-book and advocate caveats stated. (2) The wiki already covers the rent-versus-quasi-rent dispute, the mechanisms, and the capture/dissolve instruments; a Wu book page would largely duplicate data-rents, tech-rent-dissolution-vs-capture and technofeudalism, and would rest on reviews and one interview since the book text was not accessible (the Christophers page is the precedent: a stub resting on publisher copy plus reviews; the Wu page would be the same quality with less to add). (3) The better NEW page is not the book but the Tier 1 research behind its Amazon-ad argument: O'Reilly, Strauss & Mazzucato, 'Algorithmic attention rents' (Data & Policy 2024) with its Amazon companion 'Amazon's Algorithmic Rents' (UCL IIPP 2023); Mazzucato is already Tier 1 and has a people page, the wiki has no coverage of this paper, and it measures the very 'placement fee' Wu calls Amazon's master stroke. Recommend queueing that paper as its own item (full text must be fetched by a pass with access; direct curl returned 403). Optional later: a NEW research/wu-age-of-extraction.md stub only if a writer obtains the book text and wants a page-cited anchor for several inbound sentences; if so it needs >=2 inbound links (data-rents, tech-rent-dissolution-vs-capture) and should be categorised research/, not books/ (books/ is for Floyd's private library).
claim_grade: D for Wu's central thesis (interpretive/argumentative: that dominant platforms' fees are monopoly rent, and that extraction drives inequality, resentment and authoritarianism); Tier 1 source (see tier note). B for the fee-share and revenue figures, but these are third-party figures that Wu cites, and their origin sources are Tier 2 advocacy/trade analysts (ILSR; Marketplace Pulse), so on the wiki they carry as 'one advocacy group's estimate', not as established magnitudes. Tier note under EDITORIAL 4c: Tim Wu is not in people-tiers.json. Judged by the rubric: Julius Silver Professor of Law, Science and Technology at Columbia Law School since 2006 (CV), peer-reviewed law-review output (e.g. Columbia L. Rev., U. Penn. L. Rev. with Hemphill on nascent competitors), clerked for Breyer and Posner, coined 'net neutrality', author of The Master Switch (2010, canonical in the field) and The Curse of Bigness (2018): a recognised scholar in antitrust and information-industries law, so Tier 1 for (a) what antitrust history/law has been and (b) his own argument and definitions, attributed. Caveats the T1 editor should keep: he is a law professor, not an economist or a measurement source; The Age of Extraction is a 224-page Knopf trade book with endnotes, not peer-reviewed; he is an avowed neo-Brandeisian policy advocate and former Biden NEC official (Washington Monthly calls him a founding father of the movement), so 'platform fees are rent' should be written as 'Wu argues', and not as a finding; Washington Monthly's reviewer found the five-step inequality-to-authoritarianism sequence 'a sort of natural law' with little empirical support. Do not cite the book as evidence for the size of platform rents.

content_summary.thesis: Dominant platforms (Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple; extended to private-equity medical roll-ups and corporate single-family-rental landlords) have moved from an 'enablement' phase (cheap, open, useful) to an 'extraction' phase in which, having locked in both sides, they raise fees and degrade quality. Wu's own definition: extraction is monopoly rent. In the Lawfare interview (12 Nov 2025) he says he took the term from microeconomics: 'in microeconomics, people talk about monopoly extracting rent. So a rent extracted by a monopolist' and that it is 'the amount of money you're able to extract based on having monopoly power, having lack of some kind of competitor or something else disciplining you.' (Lawfare Daily transcript; quote trimmed to under 50 words each.) Same interview: 'The first half of their life was building a better product. The second half of their life has been extraction.' When pressed by Rozenshtein on where fee ends and extraction begins ('the key conceptual hinge'), Wu offered a structural rather than price test (long-held monopoly, little quality improvement, record of destroying rivals) - the interviewers and ppc.land note the line remains hard to draw (Rozenshtein: claims of decay can be 'a little vibes-based').
content_summary.structure_and_chapters: Three parts (Washington Monthly describes two main parts plus solutions): Part I platform history and the enablement-to-extraction story; Part II political/economic consequences; Part III 'Some Solutions' (p.125). Chapter titles per a retailer TOC found by search (page numbers from that listing, unverified against the book): The Genius of the Ancient City Square (13); Platformization (22); The Golden Age of Tech Optimism (41); From Enablement to Extraction (48) - the Amazon Marketplace story; Scale as a Weapon (58); The Great Harvest (66); A Long Slow Bet on Laziness (73); Big Data, Knowing the Future and Controlling (82); Artificial Intelligence and the Calculus (89); Platform Power Beyond Tech (103) - private-equity medicine and Invitation Homes rental housing; Part III: The Persistent Dream of the Self-Correcting Market (135); The Technological (142, title truncated in listing, apparently on crypto); Mere Redistribution (152); Platforms and the Architecture of Equality (159); Epilogue (173). Some titles in that listing are truncated.
key_figures_with_named_sources: Amazon's cut of third-party seller revenue: 19% in 2014, 30% in 2018, 34% in 2021 (ILSR, Stacy Mitchell, 'Amazon's Toll Road', Dec 2021, key findings; ILSR is an advocacy research group = Tier 2). ILSR also estimates Amazon seller-fee revenue (including seller advertising) of $60bn in 2019, $90bn in 2020, projected $121bn in 2021, and seller advertising at 4.6% of seller revenue in 2021 (3.4% in 2020, 1.1% earlier year as printed in the report). ILSR's later figure of 45% for the first half of 2023 is reported by ppc.land and was not located in a primary ILSR document.

Washington Monthly's summary of the book (Lowman, 2 Nov 2025): Wu gives about 19% of seller revenue as the 2014 Amazon fee, 'more than 50 percent' by 2023, and says sellers paid Amazon more than $56bn per year by 2024 'to make their products visible'. These are the reviewer's relay of the book; the book's own sourcing for them is not seen (the 50% figure matches Marketplace Pulse, Feb 2023: a typical seller pays a 15% referral fee, 20-35% fulfilment, up to 15% advertising/promotion; Marketplace Pulse = industry analyst, Tier 2/3). The $56bn is presumably Amazon's reported 2024 advertising revenue, which is not all paid by third-party sellers; treat as unverified.

Counter-view on the same data (Marketplace Pulse, same article): 'Amazon fees pay for a lot of value; whether they are too costly or have risen too fast is subjective' and the 15% referral fee has been unchanged for a decade while fulfilment and advertising fees rose. This is the quasi-rent / paid-for-services reading in a source Wu's critics use. Amazon itself disputes the advertising-harm claim (ppc.land reports inflation-adjusted cost per click flat 2019-2024; company statement, secondary).

Other platform take-rates in Washington Monthly's critique (the reviewer's own list of examples the book omits, not Wu's figures): Google ad-tech fees ~30% of publisher ad revenue; Apple in-app commission up to 30%; Uber take rate 40-70% on some fares. Reviewer gives no primary citations in the text read; do not use without finding sources (Google ad-tech share: US v. Google ad tech liability ruling, E.D. Va., April 2025; Apple: Epic v. Apple orders).

Private-equity medicine (Prospect's account of the book): one study found PE acquired more than 1,000 medical practices 2012-2021; study not named in the review. Housing: Invitation Homes and 'junk fees' (application, pet, turnover, utility-management, air-filter, smart-home fees) per Prospect/Washington Monthly. Wiki adjacency: august-rental-financialization, zimmerman-anderson-realpage-algorithmic-rent.

Tier 1-grade research the book's Amazon argument parallels: Tim O'Reilly, Ilan Strauss & Mariana Mazzucato, 'Algorithmic attention rents: a theory of digital platform market power', Data & Policy (Cambridge) 2024 (UCL IIPP WP 2023) and Rock, Strauss, O'Reilly & Mazzucato, 'Behind the clicks: can Amazon allocate user attention as it pleases?' (Int. J. Industrial Organization, 2024). Per ppc.land and a search snippet (not read in full): an ad lifts a product the platform's algorithm ranks lower by a median of 17 positions (range 5-50), and 'Amazon's ad business appears simply to be an additional fee levied on merchants rather than providing added value to them'. Whether Wu cites this is not known.
content_summary.wu_argument_vs_cited_data: Wu's own: the enablement-to-extraction life cycle; extraction = monopoly rent; 'placement fee' (sponsored results) as Amazon's 'master stroke' and a 'pure example of valueless wealth extraction' (Prospect quoting the book); the Charles River Bridge (built 1786, paid off by the 1820s, tolls continuing) as the historical model of an 'extraction machine' (Prospect) - a toll-bridge image with obvious Georgist resonance (location monopoly) that the wiki could exploit; the five-step sequence monopolisation -> extraction -> mass resentment -> democratic failure -> strongman, called 'the real road to serfdom' (also his Liberties essay, Winter 2025); the remedy set ('architecture of equality'): antitrust, utility-style regulation and price caps (e.g. EU swipe-fee caps), common-carrier non-discrimination, structural separation/'line of business' quarantines (including keeping platforms out of AI infrastructure), per Washington Monthly. Quote with locator (Prospect): 'An anti-monopoly program does not "create" competition. Instead, it takes away the most convenient tools for killing it.' Data from others: ILSR and Marketplace Pulse fee shares; the PE-medicine study; the O'Reilly/Strauss/Mazzucato attention-rent work (if cited).
content_summary.reception_and_criticism: Positive: NYT Book Review (Szalai: 'an intelligent and useful guide to a dispiriting present' per the quote on the PRH page), Financial Times (Diane Coyle, 'a must-read' per PRH page; full review not reached), New Yorker Best Books of 2025, Kirkus (positive, 'brisk, 30,000-foot view'), Publishers Weekly (starred), endorsements from Acemoglu, Lina Khan, Stoller, Doctorow, Klobuchar. Critical: Washington Monthly (thin empirical support, omits Google ad-tech and Apple commission examples, 'retread familiar intellectual territory'); Kate Klonick (Lawfare) that utility regulation is 'the opposite of an antitrust solution' (Wu: 'I reject the idea that they're opposites'); onStrategy and others that the book underplays consumer surplus; a US court (Boasberg, 18 Nov 2025) rejected the FTC's Meta monopolisation case, finding TikTok and YouTube compete (ppc.land, secondary; the wiki's tech-rent-dissolution page already carries this).

existing_wiki_coverage: Platform-rent theory is already well covered; Wu adds a named antitrust-scholar voice and a few figures, not a new topic. (1) concepts/data-rents.md: the rent vs quasi-rent dispute, network effects/data/gatekeeping, data-monopsony, remedies menu. It names no antitrust-law scholar and has no take-rate evidence. (2) concepts/taxing-tech-rents.md (48 KB): instrument comparison (ACE/DBCFT, DST, Romer ad tax, data dividends, dissolution, AI taxes, equity stakes) - mentions Amazon fee rises only as DST incidence (+2% UK, +3% France; Muddasani & Langenmayr: Amazon raised fees by about half the DST). (3) research/tech-rent-dissolution-vs-capture.md: DMA fines, US v Google remedies (Mehta, Sept 2025), FTC v Meta loss (Nov 2025), counter-case; no mention of Wu, Lina Khan, neo-Brandeisian movement, common carrier/structural separation, or price caps. (4) research/dma-interoperability-dissolution.md and research/furman-review-digital-competition.md: the official diagnosis and the interoperability remedy. (5) research/rochet-tirole-two-sided.md (tipping/pricing theory), research/korinek-ng-digital-superstars.md (Fixed-cost/zero-marginal-cost superstar mechanism; explicitly not network effects), superstar-firms, autor-superstar-firms, crouzet-eberly-intangibles (efficiency counter), de-loecker-eeckhout markup pages. (6) concepts/rentier.md (generic extension of rentier to platforms; Mazzucato, Standing, Hudson) and research/christophers-rentier-capitalism.md (stub resting on publisher copy; mentions digital platforms in a list) and research/mazzucato-mapping-rents.md (three-domain framework, platforms as one). (7) concepts/technofeudalism.md (Lanier, Varoufakis, Durand; 2026 Norris-Espinosa exchange): the polemical feudal framing; Wu's 'real road to serfdom' and toll-bridge/agora lineage is a close cousin. (8) concepts/monopsony.md, research/boldrin-levine-against-intellectual-monopoly, concepts/ip-rents. (9) research/digital-services-taxes.md and digital-services-tax-incidence.md (Amazon pass-through). (10) research/soil-to-servers-digital-rents.md (MDPI Land 2025). GAPS: no page on Amazon marketplace take-rates or on algorithmic attention rents (O'Reilly-Strauss-Mazzucato); no coverage of the Charles River Bridge / toll-infrastructure lineage; no treatment of common-carrier/utility-style price regulation as a rent-dissolution instrument (relevant to the Georgist 'natural monopoly' and public-utility tradition); no people page for Tim Wu, Lina Khan or Brett Christophers (people/ has Mazzucato, Lanier, Hudson, Standing, Weyl, Eric Posner, Josh Ryan-Collins; no Varoufakis; a Wu page would be one of the few non-Georgist-adjacent figures with no wiki-specific content to hold). Search of all .md for 'Tim Wu', 'Age of Extraction', 'Master Switch', 'Lina Khan', 'Algorithmic Attention', 'Stacy Mitchell' returned no wiki-page hits (only an unrelated inbox discovery list naming ILSR). A Wu book page would therefore be additive in labelling but duplicative in substance: it would restate the rent reading already on data-rents/technofeudalism.

uncertainties: Book text not read. Everything about content comes from publisher copy, five reviews (Prospect, Washington Monthly, Kirkus, onStrategy, ppc.land synthesis) and one long interview transcript. Figures attributed to the book (19% in 2014, over 50% by 2023, $56bn per year in 2024) are the Washington Monthly reviewer's relay and were not matched to the book's endnotes. The $56bn may be Amazon's total 2024 advertising revenue, not only seller-paid fees.

ILSR 2023 update (45% in H1 2023) not found in a primary ILSR document; only the 2021 report (19/30/34%) was read. Definitions of 'cut' differ: ILSR includes seller advertising and FBA fees; Marketplace Pulse sums referral, fulfilment and advertising from sampled seller P&Ls; neither is audited data and Amazon disputes the framing.
O'Reilly-Strauss-Mazzucato figures (median 17-position boost) are second-hand; the PDFs returned 403. Must be re-fetched (Cambridge Core open access, UCL IIPP, ResearchGate) before any wiki use.
Chapter list and page numbers come from a search-result TOC, partly truncated; titles of two chapters are incomplete.

Whether Wu cites Georgist or classical rent theory (Ricardo, George) is unknown; no review mentions it. His rent usage appears microeconomic (monopoly rent), not Ricardian scarcity rent, so the wiki should not describe the book as Georgist or as an application of land-rent theory; it fits the 'monopoly rent' gradient step, which the wiki treats as more contested than land.

Dated items in the ppc.land synthesis (2026 FTC suit against Amazon on advertising surcharges, Brinkema's Sept 2026 ad-tech ruling, Apple EU commission change) were not independently verified and should not be used without primary sources; the ppc.land page itself is trade press (Tier 3 for facts).

Tier assignment for Wu is a judgement under 4c (not in people-tiers.json); the T1 editor may prefer to add him to tier1_confirmed with a note 'law-professor Tier 1 for antitrust history and his own argument; advocate-author, so rent-claim as proponent'.
Aggregator/blog review at theworthyhouse.com (a partisan commentator) and goodreads/blinkist pages were not used and are Tier 3.
